weekly homeworks - mostly fill in the blank vocabulary type things which were easy(if you understood what was being asked which was not given), a couple coding homeworks which were a lot harder

Super straightforward lectures and organized into distinct units. First half of the semester was extremely easy as it is more conceptual and logic based, whereas the second half of the semester is harder if you don't memorize syntax. If you go to lecture, you literally don't need to study at all to get a good grade. Do the homework to study for the quiz and you're set. His style of questions is consistent and there are no curveballs. 

More detail about the HW: 11HWs, 9 written + 2 coding. The written hws take ~20-30 min on avg if you know what you're doing, maybe ~1-2hrs if you need to look through notes/slides consistently. Coding HWs are a little longer but you can do them with a partner. Takes ~2-4 hrs if you do it alone.

Lectures are always recorded and although they may be dry, reading through the slides makes sense and pretty easy to follow along. Funny guy if you like dry humor.

Although it may not feel like a crazy amount of information, most of it is quite practical/I've interacted with it while working. It'll give you a good foundation.
I guess it's an easy but a bit boring class. The exams are a bit tedious because the grading is nitpicky.

Great Professor, I had him for both CMSC424 and 436. As long as you show up to class to understand lecture (the videos can be a little hard to understand sometimes), pay attention, do the HWs (which are very straightforward), and study for quizzes and exams ahead of time, you will most likely get an A. The content you need to know is straight from the slides, nothing ever is there to trick you. Sometimes if he makes the midterm too easy, he might give a harder quiz, but it all balances out. The projects in 424 specifically can be pretty cool to do when you get to coding, the HWs are fairly straightforward too

Herve is super friendly, like genuinely one of the nicest guys at UMD. I overslept for a quiz once and I emailed him asking if there was anything I could do, and because he's so kind he just let me make it up with a small penalty. On top of that he gave me chances to submit the right assignment, and hes just a good teacher in general so I would recommend.

This was the hardest CMSC4xx class I've taken, but this is the most I've learned in a CS class at UMD. Abadi is an incredibly knowledgeable professor and wants you to learn. I enjoyed the projects quite a bit, from mastering SQL to writing a B+ tree in Java. Both TAs were also great and put a ton of work into answering Piazza questions and providing support during the projects.

Yes, this class is hard and requires a ton of investment to learn the material. There are graded clicker questions each class and exams are extremely difficult (Abadi likes to say getting questions wrong is another form of learning the material). The midterm was curved by about 15%.

I've heard that Herve teaches an easier version of the course. However, if you have the time and put in the effort, take it with Abadi and I guarantee you will walk away from this class with so much knowledge applicable to software engineering.
Just read the slides it's all you have to do. And he gives practice quizzes and exams that tell you exactly what to expect. Nice guy

It's a very chill class with him and he teaches fairly well. However, a third of the content that was on quizes or exams were based on straight memorization like do you remember the library that allows you to do this. Also, the wording on the last quiz, homework, and exam was a bit confusing and very stubborn in terms of accepting a different interpretation of his vague questions. Other than those 2 complaints it's a chill class.

Not too bad overall. While the course material is incredibly useful, the lectures can be quite dry and confusing, so I mainly studied the material using the slides or on my own. The professor is clearly organized, but the quality of class resources is inconsistent: some slides are excellent, while others are messy, and the lack of pre-populated databases makes it difficult to follow along with live examples.

The workload is fair, as the homework reflects the lecture topics well, and the first three quizzes are great for understanding the material, though the last two are quite memorization-heavy. While the exams are fair and include a clear topic breakdown, the 35% weighting of the final felt unnecessarily high. Overall, it’s a very manageable and useful class; you'll do fine.

The rest of the reviews are true, I only took 424 with Abadi since Herve's sections are full and I do not recommend it. There is no mandatory reading quizzes anymore but they're used for supplemental learning. There are clicker questions every class so attendance is mandatory and the exams are what the other reviews detail (extremely hard). There's a significant curve for each exam to help offset the difficulty. This course is a real pain in the a** so unless you want to devote your entire semester to this course, choose a different professor.

Nice guy and mostly chill class. Just be careful not to slack off, because the end of the semester is much harder than the beginning. We spent like 2 months on SQL and then covered implementation details (B+ trees, indexing, merge sort, etc.) during the last few weeks. Quizzes and exams are fair, though do keep in mind that old/practice ones won't cover everything you'll be assessed on.

name: CMSC424
title: Database Design
description: Prerequisite: Minimum grade of C- in CMSC351 and CMSC330; and permission of CMNS-Computer Science department. Or must be in the (Computer Science (Doctoral), Computer Science (Master's)) program. Students are introduced to database systems and motivates the database approach as a mechanism for modeling the real world. An in-depth coverage of the relational model, logical database design, query languages, and other database concepts including query optimization, concurrency control; transaction management, and log based crash recovery. Distributed and Web database architectures are also discussed.
